pr_title: Avoid lock contention in common MemberInfoCache code paths
pr_comments: Do we have protection in dotnet/performance, or is it worth adding your test there?

@dotnet/dotnet-perf Do you think it's worthwhile to add a test for this scenario? The raw throughput of single-threaded accesses isn't terribly interesting, but we do want to make sure we don't regress things by introducing lock contentions in concurrent access situations.

This gap looks big enough that a perf test would catch it if we reintroduce contention, so the test is a good idea. It's also something that is hard to write an assertion for, so a heuristic like this is a good idea.

issue_context.title: Lock contention on highly concurrent use of MethodBase.GetMethod
issue_context.body:
Reported as a [.NET Framework issue](https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/content/problem/703549/lock-contentionconvoy-on-highly-concurrent-use-of.html) and found with [Entity Framework](https://github.com/dotnet/ef6/issues/1172).

The same lock (through [Monitor.Enter](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/5cd7e970487c4cc9ae652185a2f867159c48c9a0/src/coreclr/src/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/RuntimeType.CoreCLR.cs#L372)) occurs in .NET Core, so created this issue to track a fix in .NET Core first, then perhaps port to .NET Framework pending outcome and priority.

A potential fix was suggested:
_The corresponding methods in MethodBase.GetProperties has a similar cache which is implemented slightly differently. In particular the method returns without trying to add the result to the cache, if the result originated from the cache. The approach should also be used in GetMethod._

cc @GrabYourPitchforks @tarekgh
comments:
We faced exactly the same problem on our production servers! There was ~900 threads, waiting for : 
```
000000CA025FD688 00007ff8d0296594 [HelperMethodFrame_1OBJ: 000000ca025fd688] System.Threading.Monitor.ReliableEnter(System.Object, Boolean ByRef)
000000CA025FD7E0 00007ff84a8914e2 System.RuntimeType+RuntimeTypeCache+MemberInfoCache`1[[System.__Canon, System.Private.CoreLib]].Insert(System.__Canon[] ByRef, System.String, MemberListType)
000000CA025FD850 00007ff84ac031e6 System.RuntimeType+RuntimeTypeCache+MemberInfoCache`1[[System.__Canon, System.Private.CoreLib]].AddMethod(System.RuntimeType, System.RuntimeMethodHandleInternal, CacheType)
000000CA025FD8D0 00007ff84ac02eb3 System.RuntimeType.GetMethodBase(System.RuntimeType, System.RuntimeMethodHandleInternal)
000000CA025FD9B0 00007ff84b956b6c System.RuntimeType.GetMethodBase(System.RuntimeType, System.IRuntimeMethodInfo)
000000CA025FD9F0 00007ff84d3fa839 System.Reflection.RuntimeMethodInfo.GetGenericMethodDefinition()
```

We actually caught a lock convoy on our production servers due to this issue. Despite the fact that the bottleneck is usually the query to the database, we still ran into this.
The solutions so far are as follows:
1. Generate expressions manually
2. Use the Compiled Query Technique
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/framework/data/adonet/ef/language-reference/compiled-queries-linq-to-entities

For our application, these solutions will require a huge refactoring and worsen the readability of the code.
Moreover, the problem is not limited to ORM. Expressions with closures are widely used.
@tarekgh Do you have any gut feel on whether this would be a candidate for backporting? I think you were involved in some other backporting conversations.

@GrabYourPitchforks do you mean backporting to the Full Framework? or previous versions of .NET Core? 

This depend if there is a customer blocked by that and there is no easy workaround can be applied. from what I am reading this is not meeting the servicing bar. we should fix it in 5.0 and if we get any complaint in the future we can back port at that time.
Should've clarified - Full Framework servicing. Thanks for the tip. Let's try this out in 5.0 for now and see how things pan out.

review_comments: Nit, this method could maybe use `Debug.Assert(Monitor.IsEntered(this))` at the top
Honestly I wanted to make this a normal `lock`. :)

Such asserts do seem to find bugs from time to time, there was one we fixed a couple months ago. So I guess there can sometimes be value in using Monitor to make this possible when a lock protects callees.
One could imagine an analyzer validating it one day?

I always find it hard to reason about volatile. For writes "If a read or write appears before this method in the code, the processor cannot move it after this method."

But all of the relevant code that appears before this method in the code is within a lock. Could you help me understand what bad scenario is possible without the memory barrier here?

I don't think anything bad can happen in practice due to some JIT implementation details. But _in theory_ without this volatile write one thread could publish a `MemberInfo` instance whose construction is not yet seen as complete. Normally this would be guarded by the lock, which provides a full memory barrier. But since we've introduced a code path which traverses this array outside the lock, we need the volatile write here to ensure the reader never sees a partially published instance.

Again, I don't think it's absolutely necessary since I'm pretty sure as an implementation detail the JIT always makes all reference-type writes volatile. But I don't know if we actually say that as an ironclad guarantee anywhere, so seems better to be safe here.
